_comment: Shader effects: what the pause menu's Shaders page offers. shader_overlay.gd builds one effect per entry, and settings_menu.gd turns each param into a row under the shader's own heading. The order of the entries here is the order of the picture: every world entry is drawn at the world's own depth in the stack, under the HUD, and every screen entry over the finished screenful, so a later entry of a kind draws over an earlier one of that kind but a world entry is under a screen entry wherever the two sit in this list. 'id' keys this effect's saved state in user://settings.cfg (section [shaders], keys '<id>_enabled' and '<id>_<param key>'), and 'enabled' is what a fresh install starts with. Param types: 'float' reads min/max/step (a slider row, with an optional 'suffix' shown after the value) and 'bool' is a toggle row. The uniform each param drives is the param's own 'key', so a shader's uniforms, this list and the saved keys all carry the same names. The 'kinds' list above is the kinds of effect this file may hold, in the order the Shaders page lists them, each with the name its category is given there; an effect's own 'kind' (defaulting to 'screen' when absent) says which one it is. The page is grouped by them, so two effects that are two different kinds of thing do not read as one list - a picture laid over the frame and the world's own geometry are not the same kind of thing, and a player looking for the switch that curves the ground should not have to find it under a CRT's heading - and a kind with no entries in 'shaders' does not appear at all, which is what makes the next kind a shader and an entry rather than a page of code. The kinds themselves: a 'screen' effect is a full-screen post-process, it names a 'shader', and the overlay gives it a layer of its own drawn over the frame beneath it. A 'vertex' effect is the world's own geometry moved by its vertex shader: it names no shader and gets no layer, and instead lists the 'materials' whose shaders it drives and the 'enable_key' uniform the list's switch is pushed to as 1 or 0, because a material has no visibility to hide. A 'world' effect is a pass over the world's own picture: it names a 'shader' and gets a layer of its own like a screen effect, but that layer is drawn at the world's depth in the stack, over the 3D world and under every HUD element, so what it reads is the world with no HUD in it and what it writes is put back under one. That is the difference between grading the terrain and grading the screenful: an outline belongs on the rock rather than on the hotbar, and a screen effect laid over the hotbar is a choice the CRT makes on purpose. A vertex effect's params drive uniforms of those materials, and each param only has to exist on one of them - the water's ripple is declared by the water material alone - which is why the overlay warns when a param exists on none rather than on any. Where a param's unit is the screen rather than the world, its label says so: the CRT's 'picture_scale' is screen pixels per dot of the picture, not a count of lines, so a dot is always a whole number of the screen's pixels and one value means the same thing at every window size (on a 960-pixel-tall window: 1x is the frame itself, 2x is 480 lines, 4x is 240 - the raster of a late-90s set - and 8x is 120). Where a param's unit is the picture, it says that too: the CRT's mask pitch is picture pixels per phosphor triad. And where it is the world, it says blocks: the bend's radius is the distance at which the bend has bitten, and the horizon's is the radius of the planet the world is bent onto, both in the same blocks the terrain is counted in. A vertex effect's own culling has a second contract with the engine - a vertex shader runs after the engine has decided what to draw, so the boxes chunks are culled against have to be grown by the same arithmetic (see src/core/world_cull.hpp) - and the knobs that contract needs are named in shader_overlay.gd, not here: this file is what the menu offers, and the water's ripple is a knob the menu offers and the culling does not want.
